title: The fish that spat its answer
hook: An archerfish spits its answer: can a fish tell human face images apart?
paper_title: Discrimination of human faces by archerfish (Toxotes chatareus)
citation: Newport, Wallis, Reshitnyk & Siebeck (2016), Scientific Reports 6:27523
summary: Two separate four-fish experiments found learned discrimination of a familiar unrewarded human face image from novel alternatives. The second cohort succeeded when colour, mean brightness and outer head shape were standardized. These trained choices do not demonstrate recognition of owners.
evidence_note: Only two faces were shown per trial. The 44 and 18 counts describe pools of novel images. Biological replication was four fish per experiment, with repeated trials and a restricted set of still frontal face images.

evidence.design: Two separate four-fish cohorts of Toxotes chatareus used food-rewarded two-alternative choice by spitting at an overhead screen. Experiment 1 tested avoidance of a familiar negative face against a pool of 44 new faces; Experiment 2 used four new fish, 18 new faces, grayscale images, an oval mask and normalized mean brightness. All subjects had prior monitor-spitting experience.

claims.claim: Archerfish hit targets above water with water jets; the face study used this response to report choices.
claims.location: Introduction final paragraph; Results Experiment 1; Methods General procedure, Fig.1C.

claims.claim: Four fish learned a rewarded and an unrewarded face; the overhead screen showed two alternatives per trial.
claims.location: Results Experiment 1; Methods General procedure and Training/testing Experiment 1.

claims.claim: In Experiment 1 the familiar unrewarded face was paired with one novel face at a time from a pool of 44; the fish discriminated above chance.
claims.location: Results Experiment 1 paragraphs 2–3 and Fig.2; Methods Training/testing Experiment 1.

claims.claim: Experiment 2 used four new fish, a pool of 18 novel faces, greyscale images, a common oval mask and normalized mean brightness.
claims.location: Results Experiment 2; Methods Stimuli and Training/testing Experiment 2.

claims.claim: The controlled cohort also discriminated the trained negative face from the new alternatives above chance.
claims.location: Results Experiment 2: GLMM Z=6.794, P<0.001; Fig.3.

claims.claim: Each experiment had only four trained laboratory fish; images were still frontal views, so recognising owners was not tested.
claims.location: Results sample-size statement; Methods Subjects and Stimuli; Discussion final paragraphs.

claims.claim: Learned discrimination of fine differences in unfamiliar face images demonstrates flexible visual abilities without identifying the specific cues or subjective understanding.
claims.location: Discussion first two paragraphs and interpretation paragraphs before frontal-view limitation.

limitations: Two separate cohorts of four fish; repeated trials are not additional animals or independent laboratory replications.
The testing rule was avoid a familiar unrewarded face and choose the other image, not choose an owner from a simultaneous array of 44 people.
Food-reward learning after prior monitor-spitting training; spontaneous social recognition was not studied.
Only still frontal views from a restricted set of rendered female human faces; owner recognition and emotions are outside this study.
Colour, brightness and head outline were controlled, but the exact remaining visual cues and neural mechanism were not identified.
The living-fish reference photograph is from a separate 2018 study; no actual footage from the 2016 face experiment is used.
The source contains training-session and model-link reporting inconsistencies documented in evidence; neither is used in narration.
evidence.correction_check: Title/DOI searches for correction, erratum and retraction and original Nature/PMC/PubMed records checked on 2026-11-13; no linked notice found. This is a dated search, not a guarantee of absence.
evidence.access_note: Read complete original main paper through PMC, including both experiments, all figure captions, full Discussion and Methods; independently verified the selected related-study photograph species, panel identity and CC BY rights. Source inconsistencies are recorded and excluded from narration.

editorial_story.audience: Curious adults who know fish visually but may not expect a trained fish to distinguish human face images.
editorial_story.subject: Toxotes chatareus archerfish choosing between human face images by spitting a water jet at an overhead screen.
editorial_story.setting: Two controlled laboratory experiments, each using four trained fish, paired face images and food rewards.
editorial_story.opening_context: The opening names an archerfish and its water jet while showing a correctly identified reference animal, then explains why that visible action can report a choice.
editorial_story.normal_expectation: A fish targets prey with water jets; a human face image is an unfamiliar target whose subtle visual differences might seem beyond this hunting skill.
editorial_story.story_selection: The observable spit response turns a cognitive question into a clear action, and a two-choice test plus separate controlled cohort supports a surprising result without claims about owners or emotions.
editorial_story.decisive_limit: Small trained laboratory cohorts discriminated restricted still frontal images; the exact cues and recognition of people in natural encounters were not established.
editorial_story.question: Can an archerfish use its visual abilities to distinguish human face images?
editorial_story.why_it_matters: It reveals flexible visual learning while showing how carefully animal cognition claims must follow the task actually tested.
editorial_story.narrative_arc: Water-jet hunter; overhead two-face choice; food/no-food learning; novel-face transfer; qualitative above-chance result; independent cohort with simpler cues controlled; continued discrimination; spoken small-sample and owner-recognition limit; return to living fish.
editorial_story.closing_payoff: The fish learned fine differences between unfamiliar face images: a result about visual discrimination, bounded by the controlled task.

posts.caption:
A fish that spits its answer: can archerfish tell human faces apart?

In two laboratory experiments, separate groups of four Toxotes chatareus learned which face image earned food and which to avoid. During testing, the familiar unrewarded face was paired with one new face at a time, drawn from a pool of 44 images in the first experiment. The fish discriminated above chance.

Four different fish also succeeded with 18 novel faces after colour, mean brightness and the outer head outline were standardized. Only TWO faces appeared per trial. The results show learned image discrimination; they do not demonstrate that fish recognise their owners or use the same cues as humans.

TT-008 | Newport, Wallis, Reshitnyk & Siebeck (2016), Scientific Reports 6:27523. DOI: 10.1038/srep27523
Paper, methods, limitations and full credits: https://akshaymohan16.github.io/toxic-tales-library/sources/tt-008.html

Archerfish reference photograph: Reichenthal, Ben-Tov & Segev (2018), Front. Neural Circuits 12:18, Fig.1A, CC BY 4.0, cropped; from a separate study (10.3389/fncir.2018.00018). Original conceptual task illustrations, not actual face-test footage or stimuli. Synthetic narration; official Toxic Tales logo.

visuals.finding: The planned task keeps two schematic faces per trial, labels illustrations and avoids invented accuracy graphs. Reference imagery comes from a separately credited study.

payoff.finding: The ending answers the opening with learned visual discrimination and does not turn it into a claim about recognising people.
payoff.basis: Compared the opening question with the final two spoken segments and their planned closing shots.

scope.finding: The script separates the two four-fish cohorts and identifies 44 and 18 as image pools, with still-image and owner-recognition limits spoken aloud.
scope.basis: Checked the original design and test rule; omitted disputed training-session/model-link details and selective peak-accuracy headlines.

retelling.finding: Trained archerfish learned to distinguish human face images by choosing with a water jet.
